investigations.name: SAFFIRE I–III — Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment
investigations.platform: Uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle (after ISS departure)
investigations.focus: Large-scale flame spread over spacecraft materials in microgravity, cabin O₂/CO₂ evolution, radiative heat flux.
investigations.fire_safety: First fire large enough to represent a real cabin fire; directly informs material selection, detection thresholds and cabin-atmosphere response models.

investigations.name: BASS & BASS-II — Burning and Suppression of Solids
investigations.focus: Flame spread, flammability limits and extinction of solid fuels (PMMA, cotton-fiberglass, acrylic spheres) under controlled low-speed flow and reduced O₂.
investigations.fire_safety: Shows that some materials burn in microgravity at lower flows/O₂ than predicted by 1-g tests; data on extinguishment by flow reduction or nitrogen.
investigations.query: Burning and Suppression of Solids BASS

investigations.name: SoFIE — Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction
investigations.focus: Ignition, flame growth and extinction of solid materials across pressures, O₂ levels and flow speeds — including exploration-atmosphere conditions.
investigations.fire_safety: Targets the low-pressure / high-O₂ atmospheres planned for exploration vehicles and habitats.
investigations.query: Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction SoFIE

investigations.name: SAME / SAME-R — Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment
investigations.focus: Particle-size distribution of smoke from overheated spacecraft materials (Teflon, Kapton, silicone, cellulose) in microgravity.
investigations.fire_safety: Smoke detectors are only as good as their match to real smoke: SAME data guide the design of next-generation spacecraft (and terrestrial) smoke detectors.

investigations.name: SSCE — Solid Surface Combustion Experiment
investigations.focus: Flame spread over thin paper and thick PMMA in quiescent microgravity and different O₂/pressure.
investigations.fire_safety: Early evidence that flames in still air spread slowly or self-extinguish — and that a ventilation flow changes everything.

investigations.name: MIST — Water-Mist Fire Suppression
investigations.focus: Interaction of fine water droplets with a propagating premixed flame — how mist size and density extinguish fire.
investigations.fire_safety: Basis for fine-water-mist extinguishers: low water mass, no toxic residue — used in space and in terrestrial fire protection.

investigations.name: FLEX / FLEX-2 — Flame Extinguishment Experiments
investigations.focus: Burning fuel droplets with N₂/CO₂/He diluents; discovered long-lived 'cool flames' after radiative extinction.
investigations.fire_safety: Quantifies which inert gases extinguish fires best in a cabin, and reveals hidden combustion modes after visible flames disappear.

investigations.name: Microgravity Smoldering Combustion
investigations.focus: Smoldering of polyurethane foam in microgravity and its transition to flaming.
investigations.fire_safety: Smoldering is slow, flameless and hard to detect — a classic pre-fire state for overheated equipment and foams.

investigations.name: ACME — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments
investigations.focus: Six gaseous-flame studies (soot, flame design, flammability limits, electric-field effects, burning-rate emulator).
investigations.fire_safety: The Burning Rate Emulator and flammability-limit studies feed predictive models of material flammability.
investigations.query: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments ACME

investigations.name: SPICE — Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment
investigations.focus: Smoke point (soot emission) of laminar jet flames in microgravity.
investigations.fire_safety: Soot and smoke production drive both radiation from fires and smoke-detector response.

kb.title: Why flames look different in microgravity
kb.answer:
On Earth, hot combustion gases are lighter than the surrounding air, so **buoyancy** pulls them upward and draws fresh air in from below — that is why a candle flame is elongated and yellow (hot soot glowing).

In microgravity there is **no buoyant convection**. Oxygen only reaches the flame by slow **diffusion** (or by forced ventilation), so the flame becomes **spherical, dimmer and bluish**, with less soot and a lower temperature. Without a ventilation flow, a flame can even **self-extinguish** because it suffocates in its own combustion products.

kb.title: Opposed vs. concurrent flow
kb.answer:
In a spacecraft, the **ventilation flow** replaces buoyancy: it feeds oxygen to the flame.

- **Concurrent flow** (flame spreads *with* the airflow): hot gases pre-heat the unburnt material ahead — spread is faster and the flame grows larger.
- **Opposed flow** (flame spreads *against* the airflow): heat must travel upstream — spread is slower.

SAFFIRE-I illustrates this on the same SIBAL fabric at 20 cm/s: sample S1 (concurrent) burned for ~420 s with a strong radiative signal, while S2 (opposed) burned ~70 s with a much weaker one. This is why **shutting down the ventilation** is one of the first fire responses on the ISS.

kb.title: The SAFFIRE experiments
kb.answer:
**SAFFIRE** (Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment) ignited large material samples inside uncrewed **Cygnus** cargo vehicles after they left the ISS, so that a realistic-size fire could be studied without risk to a crew.

- **SAFFIRE-I** (2016): one large SIBAL cotton-fiberglass sample, concurrent then opposed flow.
- **SAFFIRE-II** (2016): nine smaller samples of different materials and conditions.
- **SAFFIRE-III** (2017): large-scale flame spread revisited, with different ventilation.

Sensors include 4 radiometers, 12 thermocouples (plume + sample), anemometers, O₂ and CO₂ sensors and cabin pressure — all available in this dashboard.

kb.title: Generic spacecraft fire response
kb.answer:
Crewed vehicles follow mission-specific, certified procedures. In general terms, an ISS-style response is:

1. **Alarm & gather** — the crew is alerted and gathers at a safe location.
2. **Stop the ventilation** in the affected module — this removes the airflow that feeds a microgravity flame.
3. **Remove electrical power** to the suspect equipment.
4. **Don breathing masks** and monitor combustion products (CO, HCN, HCl, O₂).
5. **Extinguish** with a portable extinguisher if needed.
6. **Clean up** the atmosphere and verify before re-entry.

*FLAME DNA is a research prototype: it never replaces official procedures.*

kb.title: Oxygen, pressure and flammability
kb.answer:
Flammability depends strongly on the **oxygen concentration** (% O₂), not only on its partial pressure. Exploration vehicles and lunar/Martian habitats are planned with a **lower pressure but higher O₂ fraction** (e.g. ~8.2 psia with ~34 % O₂) to simplify spacewalks — but at 34 % O₂ more materials become flammable and flames spread faster than on the ISS (21 %).

That is exactly the risk window explored by **SoFIE** and **SAFFIRE**, and the reason NASA screens materials in the *worst-case* atmosphere they will see (NASA-STD-6001).

kb.title: The Apollo 1 lesson
kb.answer:
On 27 January 1967, a fire during a ground test of the **Apollo 1** command module killed astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee. The cabin held **100 % oxygen at ~16.7 psia**, with many flammable materials (Velcro, nylon) and an inward-opening hatch.

Consequences: a nitrogen/oxygen mix on the pad, flame-resistant materials (Beta cloth), a quick-opening hatch and rigorous **material flammability testing** — practices that still shape spacecraft and firefighter equipment today.

kb.title: What space fire research brings to Earth
kb.answer:
Microgravity removes buoyancy, so it isolates the *fundamental* physics of fire. Results transfer to Earth through:

- **Fine-water-mist extinguishers** — little water, no toxic residue (buildings, ships, data rooms).
- **Smoke detection** — particle-size data improve detectors for early, smoldering fires.
- **Firefighter equipment** — lighter breathing systems and flame-resistant protective clothing.
- **Enclosed-fire models** — SAFFIRE's O₂ depletion and CO₂ build-up inform fires in submarines, aircraft and apartments.
- **Oxygen-enriched settings** — hospitals and home oxygen therapy benefit from high-O₂ flammability data.

kb.title: How FLAME DNA's alert logic works
kb.answer:
The monitoring module uses a **multi-criteria, persistence-based** logic inspired by spacecraft practice instead of a single threshold:

- **Watch** — one signal deviates from its nominal band (could be a sensor fault).
- **Warning** — two *independent* fire signatures agree (e.g. smoke + CO) for several seconds.
- **Fire alarm** — smoke and a combustion product (CO or CO₂ rate) **plus** a thermal signature (temperature rise rate or heat flux) persist.

A single drifting sensor therefore cannot trigger a fire alarm — this reduces false alarms, which are costly on a spacecraft (fans stopped, crew interrupted).

kb.title: Cool flames (FLEX)
kb.answer: During **FLEX** on the ISS, heptane droplets kept burning *after* their visible flame went out: a low-temperature (~500–800 K) **cool flame** chemistry continued. It is invisible and produces different by-products — a reminder that 'no visible flame' does not always mean 'no combustion'.

kb.title: Limits of this prototype
kb.answer:
- SAFFIRE measurements are **real NASA data**; derived metrics (flame duration, heat-flux rise…) are computed automatically and should be checked against NASA publications.
- The live monitoring panel uses **simulated** sensors, calibrated on realistic cabin ranges and SAFFIRE trends.
- The habitat what-if model is an **illustrative scaling**, not a validated flammability model.
- FLAME DNA is **not a certified fire-detection system**.
